newsitem.title: FRANCE: French directors, ministers spar on immigration.
newsitem.headline: French directors, ministers spar on immigration.

text.p: French filmmakers sparred with a government minister on Wednesday, urging people to disobey hardline anti-immigration laws as he invited the directors to spend a month in a run-down suburb to get to grips with reality.

More than 60 directors, including the award-winning Bertrand Tavernier and Mathieu Kassowitz, have urged civil disobedience against a law requiring French citizens to report the arrival and departure of foreigners staying at their home.

"When a law is unjust and iniquitous, you have to destroy that law. We don't want to become police auxiliaries," Tavernier, known for hard-hitting thrillers, told a news conference at a cinema in the Paris students' Latin Quarter.
Virtually all directors taking part expressed concern at a local election victory by the far-right and anti-immigrant National Front in the southern town of Vitrolles at the weekend.

The centre-right government, facing a general election next year, has been spurred into tightening admission conditions for foreign residents by the rise of the Front, which advocates sending immigrants home.

Tavernier rejected a letter from Eric Raoult, junior minister for urban affairs and integration, which offered month-long billets for each of the 66 signatories to inner-city areas including Montreuil and Saint-Denis outside the capital.
"In this manifesto, you have unfortunately committed a script and casting mistake," the letter said.

"So as to better appreciate the scale of the economic and social difficulties facing our compatriates and their politicians in difficult areas, I invite you to come and live for a month in ...," it ran.

Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure wondered aloud after a cabinet meeting how the directors would react if filmgoers urged violations of laws governing generous subsidies to the French film industry. But Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy said he planned to meet the signatories.

"Their attitude is entirely unacceptable because film directors have no more right than anyone else to contravene the law, and especially, not the right to call on others to violate it," Justice Minister Jacques Toubon told RTL radio.

"They have no more right, but they have no less right to do so," retorted Tavernier. "When France is suffering, collective actions are right...especially when there are parties which should be acting in our stead," he added.

"We're ashamed of what is happening in our country," said Cedric Klapitsch, author of the hit-comedy "Chacun cherche son chat" (Everyone Is Looking For His Cat). "The institutions themselves are turning racist."

One of several recent protests against a four-year-old government crackdown on illegal immigrants, their statement published in the daily Le Monde on Tuesday says: "We are guilty, every one of us, of putting up illegal foreign residents recently...We request being probed and put on trial."
A French teacher was convicted this month of failing to report she had put up a friend from Zaire. The teacher argued she was not aware her friend's documents were not in order.

"We call upon our fellow-citizens to disobey and not submit to these inhuman laws," the film directors said in their statement, one of several recent protests against a four-year-old government crackdown on illegal immigrants.
There are about five million foreign nationals in France including about a million illegal entrants, most of them from developing countries.
